name: Queen Blue
lede: Queen's blue was one of the named shades of indigo that eighteenth-century English dyers sorted from light to dark, and the books say it was also called royal blue.

sections.title: One step on the indigo ladder
sections.body:
English dyers of the eighteenth century classified official shades of indigo-dyed cloth from light to dark [1][2]. Finlay's list reads milk blue, pearl blue, pale blue, flat blue, middling blue, sky blue, queen's blue, watchet blue, garter blue, mazareen blue, deep blue and navy blue [1]. Balfour-Paul gives thirteen shades, adding a Turkish blue between queen's blue and watchet blue [2]. Books disagree on the count, twelve against thirteen [1][2].

Balfour-Paul adds that queen's blue, also called king's blue, was also known as royal blue, a name that like navy blue has left its indigo roots behind and passed into common color vocabulary [2]. Finlay uses the list to make a different point: indigo gives very different results, so we cannot know what shade Newton had in mind for his rainbow band [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch is a mid-dark steel blue, a modern screen color [3]. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of it covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 86 works [3]. It is most common in French painting, 25 of the 3,443 French works [3]. The strongest cases include Van Gogh's *Three White Cottages in Saintes-Maries* of 1888 and Heinrich Hansen's Copenhagen view of 1836 [3]. As always these are photographs of varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors [3].
